sentence_as_it_stands: It does not show that oxygen holds up in *skin*: the one study that measured skin oxygen for hours found it halved and slow to recover, and although that study injected epinephrine with no anesthetic in a rat, nobody has done the equivalent measurement in a human wheal.

Approved: single-dose infiltration and, since the 2023 revision, three nerve blocks in adults — interscalene brachial plexus, sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa and adductor canal. Listed as not evaluated: epidural, intrathecal, intravascular and intra-articular use, and regional nerve blocks other than those three.
notes: Source: Rames' reference 18, the FDA prescribing information NDA 022496/S-044 (2023), whose title records the added adductor canal and sciatic (popliteal fossa) indications; Rames' text (PDF p. 4) also names the three labelled blocks, in a sentence whose dose figure is not copied, and says the other regional blocks are not established. The page's list comes from the 2021 label (its Sources entry says so; see F02). Nothing in the page's verdict on Exparel rests on the nerve-block list, and the D048 sentence that follows ('Intradermal injection appears nowhere …') is not contradicted by Rames, so importance is low. Only the nerve-block part is changed; the other route statements and the paracervical contraindication were not re-checked against the 2023 or later label.

page: Injectables ruled out but not tried
section: Sources › Liposomal and sustained-release › EXPAREL (bupivacaine liposome injectable suspension) — US prescribing information
sentence_as_it_stands: Approved: single-dose infiltration (age 6 and over) and interscalene brachial plexus nerve block (adults). … "EXPAREL has not been evaluated for the following uses and, therefore, is not recommended for these types of analgesia or routes of administration": epidural, intrathecal, regional nerve blocks other than interscalene brachial plexus, intravascular or intra-articular use. … the label read was the 2021 revision plus a secondary prescribing-information mirror, and a later revision may exist.
quote: Updated labeling including indications for adductor canal block and sciatic nerve block in the popliteal fossa; 2023.
corrected_wording: Approved: single-dose infiltration (age 6 and over) and, in adults, interscalene brachial plexus, sciatic nerve (popliteal fossa) and adductor canal blocks — the last two added in the 2023 revision (NDA 022496/S-044). Listed as not evaluated: epidural, intrathecal, intravascular or intra-articular use, and regional nerve blocks other than those three. The label read for this entry was the 2021 revision; a 2023 revision exists (Rames 2026, reference 18).
notes: Second place of the error in F01, in the Sources entry; it also answers the entry's own caveat that 'a later revision may exist' (the 2023 revision cited by Rames). Another page of the record, 'Permanent-Harm Risk Of The Candidates For The Urge To Tense' (as of 2026-10-01T03:15:21.643Z), already lists the Exparel label 'version of 2025-12-12 — label read: section 5' in its sources, so a newer label reading exists inside the record. The same Sources entry also carries dilution, admixture, interval and maximum-dose figures, which were not copied and are not part of this finding. Ambiguous on its natural reading, hence low: the entry discloses that it read the 2021 revision and that a later revision may exist, so as a record of that revision it is accurate; as a statement of the current label, which is how the page's main text uses it (F01), it is outdated.

page: What is still unsettled across these pages, and what would settle each one
section: Which claims rest on one study nobody has repeated › Days of skin anaesthesia from lecithin-coated methoxyflurane microdroplets
sentence_as_it_stands: Days of skin anaesthesia from lecithin-coated methoxyflurane microdroplets. Four to eight days of human skin anaesthesia, from a 1991 paper read as an abstract only. It is the only human formulation that has ever produced days rather than hours of skin block. It was never developed, nothing in the sustained-release class since comes close, and nobody has looked at why it stopped.
quote: Both LIQ865 formulations demonstrated dose-dependent hypoesthesia and hypoalgesia. The duration of analgesia ranged between 37 and 86 h.
corrected_wording: Days of skin anaesthesia from lecithin-coated methoxyflurane microdroplets. Four to eight days of human skin anaesthesia, from a 1991 paper read as an abstract only. Other sustained-release formulations have since produced skin analgesia lasting days from a single dose in humans: liposomal bupivacaine intradermally for up to two days (Grant 2004, PMID 15220782), bupivacaine microcapsules subcutaneously for at least four days (Pedersen 2004, PMID 15333431) and PLGA microparticle bupivacaine subcutaneously for one and a half to three and a half days (Jensen 2024, PMID 38482995). The methoxyflurane formulation was never developed, and nobody has looked at why it stopped.
notes: Rests on Jensen 2024, which came from Rames' reference list (ref 5); quote from its cached abstract (cache redacted only for the toxicity passage). Same idea as claim C043 on 'The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites…', already refuted by the main session on Grant 2004 and the microcapsule studies; this is its second location, on the open-question page. The record contradicts itself here: 'Injectables ruled out but not tried' (section 'The rest of the class') records the microcapsules' effects 'for at least 96 hours' and LIQ865's '37 to 86 hours', and Grant 2004's 19 to 48 hours intradermally. The 1991 study's place as the longest single-dose figure is not challenged.

page: Future Medications For Urge To Tense
section: Tier 1 — Local interventions at the one mechanism with direct evidence in you › 1. Magnesium (local injection — optimize, extend, and characterize) › Other duration-extension routes worth raising in the same conversation
sentence_as_it_stands: liposomal formulations extend local anesthetic effect from 6–8 hours to as much as 72 (Yang et al., Front Pain Res 2026). Neither has been used for this indication, but they define the space of “the same relief, lasting longer.”
quote: When infiltrated surgically and compared with unencapsulated bupivacaine or ropivacaine, only 11% of trials (4 of 36) reported a clinically relevant and statistically significant improvement in the primary outcome favoring liposomal bupivacaine.
corrected_wording: Liposomal bupivacaine is marketed as extending postsurgical analgesia to as much as 72 hours (Yang et al., Front Pain Res 2026), but in randomised trials surgically infiltrated liposomal bupivacaine beat plain bupivacaine or ropivacaine on the primary outcome in 4 of 36 trials (Ilfeld 2021, PMID 33372949), and the regulator's review of the two pivotal trials found the difference from placebo confined to the first 24 hours (as recorded on 'Injectables ruled out but not tried'). Neither has been used for this indication.
notes: Rests on Ilfeld, Eisenach & Gabriel 2021 (Anesthesiology review of 76 RCTs), which came from Rames' reference list (ref 22); quote from its cached abstract. Not the Ilfeld 2021 phantom-limb trial cited elsewhere in the record. The same bullet list on this page already gives Zadrazil 2024 as a counterweight (correctly summarised), so the page is not one-sided; the finding concerns only the 72-hour figure, which conflicts with the FDA quotation held on 'Injectables ruled out but not tried'. Rames itself repeats the 72-hour figure as background, citing its reference 3 (a 2010 Mohs pain survey that predates the product), so Rames is not evidence for it. Low importance: an aside on a page about a different condition. Ambiguous on its natural reading, hence low: 'extend local anesthetic effect … to as much as 72' is defensible for the drug's prolonged presence and occasional late residual block (Zadrazil 2024 reports intermittent residual sensory blockade beyond 3.5 days), but overstated as a statement of clinical relief, which is how the bullet uses it ('the same relief, lasting longer').

page: Injectables ruled out but not tried
section: Liposomal bupivacaine and the sustained-release class › The rest of the class
sentence_as_it_stands: Nothing in this class is marketed anywhere except Exparel.
quote: Prolonged-release (PR; as ascribed in the EU) or extended-release (as ascribed in the USA) bupivacaine/meloxicam (HTX-011; hereafter referred to as bupivacaine/meloxicam PR; Zynrelef) is a synergistic fixed-dose combination (FDC) of the local anaesthetic bupivacaine and the NSAID meloxicam. It is approved in the EU and the USA to treat postoperative pain.
corrected_wording: Exparel is not the only sustained-release local anaesthetic on the market. A prolonged-release bupivacaine–meloxicam solution applied needle-free to the surgical site (Zynrelef) is approved in the EU and the USA (Blair 2021, PMID 34228280) and has been used in routine care at US hospitals (Goel 2023, PMID 38698776), and a collagen implant releasing bupivacaine for up to 24 hours after inguinal hernia repair (Xaracoll) is FDA-approved and has been used in routine US surgical care (Scott 2024, PMID 38449985). Both are surgical-site products, not injectable suspensions.
notes: 'This class' is the section's sustained-release local-anaesthetic class (heading 'Liposomal bupivacaine and the sustained-release class'; the sentence closes the sub-section 'The rest of the class', after microcapsules, LIQ865 microparticles and methoxyflurane microdroplets). Sources come from a PubMed search run for this follow-up, not from Rames' reference list. Approved versus marketed: the abstracts state approval (Zynrelef: EU and USA; Xaracoll: USA, also Beaton 2023, PMID 37076252) and show routine clinical use in the USA, which implies marketing there; none states a launch date, EU marketing, or approval year (Zynrelef was approved in both regions before the July 2021 review; a 2020 meta-analysis, PMID 33487831, still called HTX-011 'yet unapproved'). The sentence was right when the 2018-era reviews were written: Balocco 2018 (PMID 30074492) calls Exparel 'currently the only extended-release formulation of bupivacaine approved by the FDA', so the kind is outdated. Not included: the sucrose-acetate-isobutyrate depot (SABER-bupivacaine), which carries the trade name Posimir in a 2022 trial abstract (PMID 35584248) but whose approval or marketing no PubMed abstract found states. Importance low: the page's exclusion of the class rests on the needle rule, the trial evidence and Mexican availability, and both products are surgical-site formulations; Mexican availability of either was not checked.
